entries.summary: One enforcement action defined the window, and it is a doctrinal shift rather than a routine citation. FDA's Sep 18 warning letter to Empower Pharmacy — reference MARCS-CMS 738238, a 503A facility inspected Nov 3–14, 2025 — found its tirzepatide/niacinamide and semaglutide/cyanocobalamin formulations to be essentially copies of approved products and stated that given production volume, the differences are 'pretextual'. Counsel read it as the first time FDA has directly engaged when customisation becomes mass-copying in a GLP-1 warning letter, and as establishing that volume alone can evidence pretext independent of documentation defects. Separately, the 503B bulks list proposal to exclude semaglutide, tirzepatide and liraglutide received NO final determination in the window despite its comment period closing July 30. No new Novo or Lilly litigation against compounders, telehealth firms or med spas was verified.
entries.content:
August 10 - September 28, 2026 compounding pharmacy:

1. FDA WARNING LETTER TO EMPOWER PHARMACY (letter dated Sep 18, posted Sep 22) - THE WINDOW'S EVENT
   PRIMARY SOURCE: FDA, reference MARCS-CMS 738238
   - Addressed to Arta Shaun Noorian, Founder & CEO, Empower Clinic Services LLC dba Empower Pharmacy,
     Houston TX - a 503A facility and one of the largest US compounded-GLP-1 suppliers
   - Inspection 3-14 November 2025; Form FDA 483 issued 2025-11-14
   - Products named: TIRZEPATIDE/NIACINAMIDE (4 mL)(17/2 mg/mL) and
     SEMAGLUTIDE/CYANOCOBALAMIN (1 mL)(5/0.5 mg/mL); a third, TIRZEPATIDE/NIACINAMIDE (2.5 mL)
     (8/2 mg/mL), also appears in the cited set. Compounded in high volumes July-October 2025.
   - FDA FINDING: these 'appear to be essentially copies of FDA-approved semaglutide and tirzepatide
     products', and 'the volume of products you are producing suggests that differences between
     products you are compounding and the FDA-approved products are pretextual'
   - FDA also cited orders lacking any prescriber determination of significant difference, and
     purported determinations 'repeated verbatim across many records'
   - FOUR VIOLATION CATEGORIES: (i) failure to meet Section 503A conditions (essentially-copies,
     inordinate amounts); (ii) adulteration under Section 501(a)(2)(A) from insanitary conditions and
     inadequate aseptic validation; (iii) unapproved new drugs; (iv) misbranding
   - Response due within 15 working days
   - FDA said it could not fully evaluate the adequacy of several corrective actions for lack of
     supporting documentation

2. WHY IT MATTERS - LEGAL READ (Frier Levitt Sep 25; AmSpa Sep 24; BioSpace Sep 24)
   *** THIS IS LAW-FIRM AND TRADE COMMENTARY, NOT A REGULATORY INSTRUMENT. These are interpretations
   of the letter, not new FDA rules. ***
   Counsel read three enforcement shifts into it:
   - PRODUCTION VOLUME ALONE can evidence pretext, independent of documentation defects
   - Templated language and pre-selected options on THIRD-PARTY PRESCRIBING PLATFORMS undermine claims
     of genuine clinical judgment
   - Verbatim 'significant difference' statements across prescriptions signal improper standardisation
   This is the first time FDA has directly engaged the question of WHEN CUSTOMISATION BECOMES
   MASS-COPYING in a GLP-1 warning letter - i.e. the core of the 'personalized dosing' loophole fight.

3. FDA FORM 483 TO CAROLINA INFUSION LLC (Aug 18)
   - Carolina Infusion, LLC (Ridgeland, SC), listed as a 503A facility, 483 dated 08/18/2026
   - The only compounding-facility 483 dated inside the window on FDA's compounding actions page
   - STATUS: INSPECTIONAL OBSERVATIONS, not a warning letter or a finding of violation
   - *** NO GLP-1, semaglutide or tirzepatide involvement could be verified. DO NOT characterise this
     as a GLP-1 action. ***

4. 503B BULKS LIST - STILL NO FINAL DETERMINATION AS OF SEP 28
   - FDA's proposal to EXCLUDE semaglutide, tirzepatide and liraglutide published in the Federal
     Register 2026-05-01 (document 2026-08552)
   - Comment period extended 2026-06-26, closed 2026-07-30
   - NO final determination published in the window
   - *** SCOPE CLARIFICATION: this is a proposal to exclude from the 503B BULKS LIST ONLY. It is NOT a
     ban on 503A compounding. ***

5. FDA SHORTAGE / ENFORCEMENT-DISCRETION STATUS: UNCHANGED IN WINDOW
   - Semaglutide shortage resolved 2025-02-21; tirzepatide resolved 2024-12-19
   - Enforcement discretion ended 2025-04-22 / 2025-05-22 (semaglutide) and 2025-02-18 / 2025-03-19
     (tirzepatide)
   - FDA's clarifying page was last updated 2026-04-01

6. VERIFIED NEGATIVES FOR THIS WINDOW
   - Novo Nordisk and Eli Lilly litigation against compounders, telehealth firms and med spas: NO new
     filings, rulings, injunctions or settlements verified inside the window. All datable events
     pre-date it: Novo's 14-lawsuit wave (announced 2025-08-05, 132 federal complaints across 40
     states), Novo v. Hims & Hers (filed 2026-02-09, dropped 2026-03-09), and Strive Compounding
     Pharmacy's antitrust suit against Lilly and Novo (W.D. Tex. San Antonio, case 5:26-CV-1055, filed
     2026-01-14). A trade-press reference to a Strive AMENDED complaint could not be dated or verified
     and is NOT published.
   - Other FDA warning-letter waves to telehealth GLP-1 marketers: the 2026 waves were 2026-03-03
     (30 letters) and 2026-06-16 (25 letters), both outside the window. NO new wave Aug 10 - Sep 28.
   - State pharmacy board actions, seizures, injunctions, grey-market API imports, counterfeit pen
     seizures: nothing verified in window. Most recent counterfeit Ozempic action found remains the
     December 2025 seizure of units labelled lot PAR1229.
   - COVERAGE CAVEAT: the negative findings for state pharmacy boards, seizures and grey-market API
     rest on fewer independent queries than intended because the search budget was exhausted. Treat as
     'none found' rather than 'none exists'.

entries.summary: The compounded-GLP-1 endgame is close but not closed. The 503B bulks comment period ended July 30 (extended from June 29) with NO final action as of Aug 8 - verified against the Federal Register API, which shows zero in-window FR documents on 503B GLP-1s. FDA's FY2027 fee notice disclosed the sector's true size: just 87 registered outsourcing facilities including 8 small businesses. The migration is essentially complete on the demand side - LifeMD stated that ~95% of all new weight-management patients now begin on branded GLP-1s and it is 'effectively at the end of its transition away from compounded.' Meanwhile FDA's own advisory committee voted 6 of 7 peptides ONTO the 503A bulks list against staff recommendation. CORRECTION: the widely-cited 3,868-comment figure could not be verified.
entries.content:
July-August 2026 compounding:

1. FDA 503B BULKS - NO FINAL ACTION (verified negative)
   - Comment period closed Jul 30, 2026 - EXTENDED from June 29 by a June 26 Federal Register notice
   - Zero FR documents mentioning semaglutide/tirzepatide/liraglutide in a 503B context published Jul 1 - Aug 8 (checked via Federal Register public API)
   - CORRECTION: the '3,868 comments' figure the dashboard carried could NOT be independently verified - regulations.gov returns HTTP 403 to all automated access and its API requires a registered key
   - Legal posture: the 503B bulks list is built through notice-and-comment NOTICES under FDCA 503B(a)(2), so the output is a final determination / list revision, NOT a codified rule
   - Final action still expected H2 2026

2. SECTOR SIZE DISCLOSED (FY2027 fee notice, Jul 30, 91 FR 48142)
   - FDA estimates 87 REGISTERED OUTSOURCING FACILITIES in FY2027, including 8 small businesses
   - That is the denominator for any 503B market model
   - FY2027 rates (effective Oct 1, 2026): small-business establishment fee $7,142; non-small-business $22,074; reinspection $21,427
   - Projected fee revenue $1,864,149

3. MIGRATION ESSENTIALLY COMPLETE (LifeMD 8-K, Aug 5)
   - Verbatim: 'Approximately 95% of all new weight management patients now begin treatment with branded GLP-1 therapies; with the guidance provided today, the Company believes it is effectively at the end of its transition away from compounded GLP-1 medications.'
   - Q2 revenue $47.3M; ~108,000 Weight Management subscribers; total subscribers +20% YoY to ~356,000; gross margin ~89%
   - BUT full-year guidance CUT to $205.5-212.5M from $220-230M - the transition has a real cost
   - LifeMD integrated with LillyDirect's pharmacy provider Gifthealth for Zepbound single-dose vials
   - WeightWatchers: clinical subscribers 197,000 (+55.7%) achieved 'despite lapping significant prior-year growth in Q2 2025 from the Company's former compounded semaglutide offering' (discontinued May 22, 2025)

4. FDA'S OWN ADVISORY COMMITTEE BREAKS WITH STAFF (PCAC, Jul 23-24)
   - Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee met at White Oak on seven peptide families
   - Recommended SIX for 503A bulks list inclusion; FDA's own briefing documents proposed including NONE
   - Day 1: BPC-157 (ulcerative colitis), KPV (wound healing), TB-500 (wound healing), MOTs-C (evaluated for OBESITY and osteoporosis)
   - Day 2: Emideltide/DSIP (rejected), Semax, Epitalon
   - This is the 503A track - no GLP-1s were on the agenda - but MOTs-C's obesity nomination puts it adjacent to the market
   - Non-binding; changes nothing until rulemaking. Follow-up PCAC expected before Feb 2027.

5. LITIGATION
   - Lilly v. Empower (S.D. Tex. 4:25-cv-03464): docket entries 106-108 all dated Aug 3 (transcript request, transcript, notice of filing) indicating a hearing occurred. NO new substantive ruling in-window; the May 16 order preserving Lanham Act claims remains operative. A second, earlier Lilly v. Empower action exists in D.N.J. (2:25-cv-02183).
   - OFA v. FDA (5th Cir. 25-10600, 25-10758): argued March 30, 2026 before Judges Richman, Duncan, Oldham; STILL UNDECIDED. Only in-window activity was administrative (Jul 7 caption substitution of Acting Commissioner Kyle Diamantas for Marty Makary).
   - FTC + Utah + California sued Hims & Hers (Jul 29, N.D. Cal.) over sharing health data with Meta/Snap, charging before promised consultations, and burying cancellation. SCOPE CAVEAT: this is NOT a compounded-GLP-1 case. HIMS fell 10%.

6. WHAT COULD NOT BE VERIFIED
   - FDA warning letters / untitled letters / import alerts to compounders in-window: fda.gov blocked every automated route. Two third-party trackers show nothing after June 8. The known 2026 waves (March 3, ~30 letters; June 8/16, ~25 telehealth letters) both predate the window. Likely genuinely absent.
   - Empower, Olympia, Hallandale, Strive, Red Rock: no dated in-window news for any. (Two widely-surfaced Empower CEO interviews are dated July 31, 2025 - a full year off.)
   - The 503A ~4-rx/month threshold: no in-window development; it traces to FDA's April 1, 2026 clarification.

7. TELEHEALTH PRICING SHIFTS (independent tracker, indicative not primary)
   - Zealthy delisted following federal enforcement against FitRX LLC
   - Ro cut annual-prepaid maintenance from $373 to $323/month and added Foundayo
   - Eden moved to $99/mo membership + $99/mo COMPOUNDED semaglutide ($198 all-in) - still selling compounded
   - Klarity Health delisted

entries.summary: The FDA 503B Bulks List comment period closed June 29, 2026 with **3,868 docket comments** received. The Alliance for Pharmacy Compounding (APC), National Community Pharmacists Association (NCPA), and dozens of telehealth compounders filed formal opposition. FDA cited >1,700 adverse-event reports tied to compounded semaglutide and tirzepatide (as of May 21, 2026) in support of its proposal. Industry expects final action in H2 2026; if finalized, would foreclose any future bulk-compounding pathway even under re-designated shortage. 503A patient-specific compounding remains legal subject to 4-rx/month threshold.
entries.content:
End-of-June 2026 — FDA 503B Bulks List comment period closure:

1. COMMENT PERIOD CLOSED (June 29, 2026):
   - Federal docket FDA-2018-N-3240
   - **3,868 docket comments received**
   - Formal opposition from APC, NCPA, telehealth compounders
   - Industry submission window now permanently closed

2. FDA SUPPORTING EVIDENCE:
   - >1,700 adverse-event reports tied to compounded semaglutide/tirzepatide (May 21 cutoff)
   - 'No clinical need' finding for 503B compounding given commercial availability
   - Hard line between clinical and economic need (price savings) for 503B

3. PATH FORWARD:
   - FDA reviews comments — typically 4-6 months
   - Final action expected H2 2026 (Q3 most likely)
   - If finalized: rule becomes effective ~30-60 days post-publication
   - Could be appealed in federal court (likely industry plaintiff)

4. 503A vs 503B STATUS POST-RULE:
   - 503B (outsourcing facilities): If finalized, bulk-compounding sema/tirz/liraglutide FORECLOSED even under shortage
   - 503A (individual patient compounding): REMAINS legal but subject to FDA's 4 rx/month enforcement threshold per April 1 guidance

5. INDUSTRY POSITION:
   - Empower Pharmacy: 4 FDA warning letters; Lilly v Empower lawsuit ongoing
   - Olympia Pharmaceuticals: 503B; existential challenge if finalized
   - Hallandale Pharmacy: 503A; less impacted but still subject to 4-rx/mo limit
   - Smaller 503A pharmacies: operating in narrowing legal space

6. PATIENT MIGRATION (continuing):
   - Bridge $50/mo + Foundayo $149 + Wegovy pill $149 + Novo subscription $249-329 = stronger branded alternatives than ever before
   - Compounded-to-branded migration estimate: 700K-1.2M patients Q2 2026
   - Hims fulfilled 125K+ branded Wegovy shipments in 6 weeks post-pivot

7. KEY READS:
   - Pharmacy Times (compounded GLP-1 sunset): https://www.pharmacytimes.com/view/fda-moves-to-permanently-close-the-door-on-compounded-glp-1s
   - APC statement: https://a4pc.org/news/apc-on-503b-glp1-proposal

entries.summary: Compounding sector status (June 24, 2026): (1) FDA 503B bulks list proposal — comment period closes June 29, 2026; NO final action issued yet; final expected Q3 2026. (2) Lilly v. Empower Pharmacy — SDTX ruled May 16, 2026, trimming but preserving Lanham Act and unfair-competition claims tied to 'untested and unapproved' compounded tirzepatide; case proceeds to full merits. (3) 503A 4-rx/month enforcement threshold continues. (4) Compounded GLP-1 patient migration to branded continues — Hims branded Wegovy fulfilled 125K shipments in 6 weeks.
entries.content:
May-June 2026 compounding pharmacy landscape:

1. FDA 503B BULKS LIST PROPOSAL (status — June 24, 2026):
   - Proposal published April 30, 2026 (Federal Register May 1)
   - Proposes permanent exclusion of semaglutide, tirzepatide, liraglutide from 503B bulks list
   - 'No clinical need' finding by FDA — clinical vs economic need distinction
   - Comment period CLOSES June 29, 2026 (5 days from now)
   - NO final action as of June 24, 2026
   - Final determination expected Q3 2026
   - If finalized: forecloses large-scale 503B compounding even under future shortage declarations

2. LILLY v. EMPOWER PHARMACY (SDTX ruling May 16):
   - Filed July 2025
   - SDTX trimmed parts of complaint but PRESERVED:
     - Lanham Act false advertising claims
     - Unfair competition claims
     - Both tied to 'untested and unapproved' compounded tirzepatide
   - Proceeds to full merits trial
   - Keeps largest 503A GLP-1 compounder exposed to liability
   - Concurrent with FDA's broader 503B bulks proposal threatening bulk-API supply

3. 503A 4-RX/MONTH ENFORCEMENT (continuing):
   - FDA April 1, 2026 clarification: 503A pharmacies filling ≤4 rx/month per essentially-copy drug face limited enforcement; above that, active enforcement
   - Empower, Hallandale, Olympia, BMI all operating under this threshold
   - Effectively kills scale economics for compounders targeting GLP-1 as mass-market product

4. PATIENT MIGRATION TO BRANDED (accelerating):
   - Hims fulfilled 125K+ branded Wegovy shipments in first 6 weeks
   - Hims projects 100K+ new weight-loss subs/month
   - WeightWatchers Sequence clinical subs +51% QoQ to 197K
   - Foundayo branded $149/mo ($25/mo with commercial savings card) — competitively priced vs compounded
   - Wegovy oral pill at $149/mo — convenience play
   - Total compounded-to-branded migration estimate: 600K-1M patients in Q2 2026

5. INDUSTRY STATUS:
   - Empower Pharmacy: 4 FDA warning letters; Lilly lawsuit proceeds; 503B exclusion looms
   - Olympia Pharmaceuticals: 503B; existential challenge if rule finalizes
   - Hallandale Pharmacy: 503A; less affected by 503B exclusion but subject to 4-rx/mo limit
   - Smaller 503A pharmacies: Operating in increasingly narrow legal space

6. OUTLOOK:
   - Q3 2026 FDA finalizes 503B exclusion → effective Q4 2026 / Q1 2027
   - Lilly v. Empower likely settles or goes to trial in 2027
   - Compounded GLP-1 industry fully sunset by end 2027 baseline scenario
   - Surviving paths: legitimate 503A individualized compounding for medical necessity (not price)

entries.summary: April 30 / May 1 federal action: FDA proposed to permanently exclude semaglutide, tirzepatide, and liraglutide from the 503B Bulks List — finding no clinical need for outsourcing-facility compounding. Federal Register publication May 1. Comment period through June 29, 2026. If finalized, this effectively ends large-scale 503B compounding of the three most-prescribed GLP-1 substances. 503A (individual patient compounding) remains legal but limited to 4 prescriptions/month per the April 1 enforcement threshold. The 'cat-and-mouse' era is ending.
entries.content:
April 30, 2026 — the FDA's hardest action against compounded GLP-1 supply:

1. THE PROPOSAL: FDA proposes to permanently exclude semaglutide, tirzepatide, and liraglutide from the 503B Bulks List. Without inclusion, 503B outsourcing facilities cannot legally compound these substances absent a shortage. Federal Register notice published May 1, 2026; comment period closes June 29, 2026.

2. FDA RATIONALE: The agency found 'no clinical need' for 503B compounding of these substances given commercial availability of FDA-approved products at affordable post-MFN prices. This draws a hard line between CLINICAL need (legitimate medical need not met by branded products) and ECONOMIC need (cost savings vs branded).

3. WHO IS AFFECTED:
   - Empower Pharmacy: Already 4 FDA warning letters; 503B GLP-1 production was material revenue.
   - Olympia Pharmaceuticals: 503B; significant GLP-1 compounding business.
   - Hallandale Pharmacy: 503A; less affected by 503B exclusion but still subject to 4-rx/month limit.
   - Various smaller 503B facilities: Existential challenge if rule finalizes.

4. 503A vs 503B DISTINCTION:
   - 503A (individual-patient compounding): Still legal for individualized medical needs. Subject to 4-prescriptions/month enforcement threshold per FDA April 1 guidance.
   - 503B (outsourcing facility): Subject to the new bulks list exclusion. If finalized, effectively ends mass-volume compounding.

5. PATIENT MIGRATION (estimated 1-1.5M US patients on compounded GLP-1s):
   - Foundayo branded $149/mo self-pay → most likely path
   - Wegovy oral pill $149/mo self-pay → strong alternative
   - MFN $245/mo Medicare → for eligible Medicare beneficiaries
   - TrumpRx $350/mo DTC → for commercially uninsured
   - Novo subscription $249-329/mo → 12-month plan offers best value

6. LEGAL POSITION OF COMPOUNDERS:
   - Outsourcing Facility Association (OFA) lawsuit over original shortage-resolution policy still pending; no favorable ruling.
   - The new 503B bulks list proposal may face additional legal challenge but FDA's 'no clinical need' finding is robust.
   - Industry expectation: FDA finalizes proposal in Q3 2026 with effective date Q4 2026 / Q1 2027.

entries.summary: April 2026 compounding update: FDA issued April 1 clarification capping 503A essentially-copy compounding at 4 prescriptions/month per compounder (the "April Fool's Day announcement" was serious). 50+ warning letters sent cumulatively. The economics have shifted dramatically: Hims raised branded Ozempic to $1,799/mo (from $199 compounded); Foundayo branded at $149/mo undercuts compounded semaglutide's traditional pricing advantage. Patient migration from compounded to branded expected to accelerate Q2-Q3 2026.
entries.content:
April 2026 compounded GLP-1 market — structural shift in progress:

1. FDA APRIL 1 CLARIFICATION (not a joke): The FDA formalized its compounding enforcement posture on April 1, 2026, setting a limited-enforcement-discretion threshold: 503A pharmacies filling ≤4 prescriptions/month per essentially-copy drug face limited FDA action; above that volume, the agency will actively enforce. This effectively destroys scale economics for compounders targeting GLP-1 as a mass-market product.

2. WARNING LETTERS: Wilson Sonsini documents 50+ FDA warning letters issued cumulatively to GLP-1 compounders and manufacturers since February 2025 shortage resolution. Recent targets include Empower Pharmacy (4th warning letter — sterile drug deficiencies), and a separate batch of 30 letters to telehealth companies in Q1 2026.

3. ECONOMIC DISRUPTION — THE $149 FOUNDAYO PIVOT: Hims raised its branded Ozempic offering to $1,799/month (up from $199 compounded) after the Novo settlement. Simultaneously, Foundayo launched at $149/month self-pay through Amazon Pharmacy, LillyDirect, and retail. The economic logic that drove compounded demand (70-90% savings vs branded) is partially inverted: Foundayo branded is cheaper than most compounded offerings. Patient migration from compounding to Foundayo expected to accelerate through Q2-Q3 2026.

4. 503B STATUS: Outsourcing facility compounding under 503B has been under enforcement since May 22, 2025. The OFA lawsuit remains pending with no court ruling favorable to compounders as of April 2026.

5. PATIENT IMPACT: An estimated 1-1.5M US patients remain on compounded GLP-1s as of April 2026, down from ~2M peak in 2024. Most likely migration path: (a) switch to Foundayo at $149/mo self-pay, (b) switch to branded Wegovy oral at $149/mo, (c) switch to branded via subscription ($249-329/mo Novo plans).

entries.summary: FDA issued an April 1, 2026 clarification: 503A pharmacies (individual patient compounding) can no longer rely on the semaglutide shortage exemption — the discretion period has ended. 503B outsourcing facilities also face tightened restrictions. DOJ referrals are now in play alongside FDA warning letters. The Hims & Hers settlement with Novo Nordisk signals compounders face both civil and criminal risk.
entries.content:
April 1, 2026 represents a regulatory turning point for compounded GLP-1 drugs in the US. Key developments:

1. FDA APRIL 1 CLARIFICATION: The FDA issued guidance reminding compounders that the period of enforcement discretion for semaglutide 503A compounding has ended. 503A pharmacies (which compound for individual patient prescriptions) must now meet strict conditions: the compounded drug must NOT be essentially a copy of a commercially available product, and there must be documented patient-specific medical need for the deviation. Adding vitamin B12 or niacinamide has been explicitly ruled out as insufficient justification.

2. 503B OUTSOURCING: Facilities compounding under 503B were already under enforcement since May 22, 2025. The FDA continues to monitor and has not relaxed its position, with active litigation from the Outsourcing Facility Association (OFA) still ongoing but no favorable court ruling as of April 2026.

3. DOJ REFERRALS: The FDA has begun referring egregious cases to the Department of Justice for criminal prosecution — escalating beyond warning letters and civil penalties. This signals that the agency views the continued growth of compounded GLP-1s post-shortage resolution as a serious public health issue.

4. MARKET IMPACT: The Hims & Hers settlement with Novo Nordisk (March 2026) effectively ended one of the largest compounded GLP-1 distribution channels. Ro (Roman), another major telehealth platform, has also wound down its compounded semaglutide program. Smaller platforms and 503A pharmacies continue to operate in the gray zone, though the legal risk has materially increased.

5. PATIENT IMPACT: An estimated 1.5-2 million US patients were receiving compounded semaglutide or tirzepatide as of Q1 2026. As platforms wind down, patients face either switching to branded products at higher cost, or losing access entirely if their insurance doesn't cover GLP-1s.

entries.summary: Legal analysis confirms that as of May 22, 2025, 503B outsourcing facilities cannot rely on the shortage exception for essentially-copy semaglutide compounding, unless ongoing litigation reverses the FDA's determination. Individual patient need exceptions remain valid for dose modifications and inactive ingredient changes. Compounders using salt forms (semaglutide sodium/acetate) face heightened legal risk as these are classified as different active ingredients.
entries.content: Sheppard Health Law's analysis clarifies the post-shortage compounding landscape with precision relevant to telehealth operators and compounding pharmacies. Key legal points: (1) The FDA's February 21, 2025 removal of semaglutide from the shortage list triggered the 503B enforcement date of May 22, 2025 — after which compounding an essentially-copy semaglutide product became illegal for 503B outsourcing facilities. (2) 503A pharmacies (individual patient prescriptions) retain rights to compound non-essentially-copy formulations for individual patient needs — including different doses, different inactive ingredients due to adverse reactions, or discontinued strengths. (3) Adding trace B12 or niacinamide does NOT create a valid individual patient need; FDA has explicitly rejected this workaround. (4) Semaglutide salt forms (semaglutide sodium, semaglutide acetate) are technically different active ingredients and are not GRAS (Generally Recognized As Safe) — compounders using these forms face FDA enforcement as an unlicensed drug product rather than a compounded drug. (5) The OFA lawsuit is still potentially active; if the court rules in OFA's favor, the shortage exception could be reinstated. As of March 30, 2026, no such ruling has occurred. This legal landscape has major implications for Hims & Hers, Ro, and other telehealth platforms that built revenue streams on compounded GLP-1s.

entries.summary: Despite FDA enforcement, unapproved compounded GLP-1s continue to grow: IQVIA data shows compounded semaglutide/tirzepatide prescriptions increased post-shortage resolution. About 80% of compounded prescriptions now include supplemental ingredients (B vitamins, niacinamide) to claim 'personalization' and avoid the essentially-a-copy prohibition. FDA created a 'green list' of API manufacturers whose facilities meet safety standards.
entries.content: Healthcare Brew's March 23, 2026 investigation reveals that the FDA's enforcement campaign has not halted compounded GLP-1 growth — in some metrics, it has accelerated it. IQVIA data from October 2025 showed that after the FDA declared the semaglutide shortage resolved in February 2025, compounded semaglutide and tirzepatide prescriptions continued to increase rather than decline. The key workaround: 'personalization.' Approximately 80% of compounded semaglutide and tirzepatide prescriptions now include supplemental ingredients — most commonly vitamin B12 or niacinamide — allowing compounders to argue their products are 'not essentially a copy' of FDA-approved drugs and therefore permissible under Section 503A. The FDA has explicitly rejected this argument, stating that adding a trace amount of B12 does not create a patient-specific medical need that justifies compounding. The agency created a 'green list' of API manufacturers whose semaglutide and tirzepatide facilities meet safety standards, and issued import alerts to detain APIs from non-listed suppliers at the border — directly attacking the supply chain rather than just the compounders. With potential seizures and injunctions threatened, the FDA's March 2026 batch of 30 warning letters to telehealth companies represents escalating enforcement, but the industry's rapid adaptation to each new rule suggests the cat-and-mouse dynamic will continue through at least the end of 2026.

On February 21, 2025, the FDA resolved the semaglutide shortage designation that had been in place since 2022, removing the legal basis for compounding copies of Ozempic and Wegovy. The FDA established wind-down periods giving 503A pharmacies until April 22, 2025 and 503B outsourcing facilities until May 22, 2025 to cease compounding. The Outsourcing Facilities Association filed a lawsuit challenging the determination as arbitrary and capricious, but a federal district court denied the preliminary injunction in April 2025. By June 2025, FDA shipping data showed semaglutide compounding shipments dropped 90% compared to June 2024, signaling rapid market contraction.
entries.summary: FDA removes semaglutide from drug shortage list, ending legal basis for compounding

entries.content: Eli Lilly filed lawsuits against Empower Pharmacy and Strive Pharmacy in April 2025, alleging they are falsely marketing compounded products as personalized versions of Zepbound and Mounjaro to circumvent the FDA's compounding ban. Empower responded that restricting access to personalized alternatives is not in the best interest of patients, and continued offering modified formulations including tirzepatide with niacinamide and oral disintegrating tablet forms. In a counter-move, Strive filed an antitrust lawsuit in January 2026 accusing Lilly and Novo Nordisk of entering exclusive agreements with telehealth platforms to suppress compounding competition. As of mid-2025, Novo Nordisk had filed over 130 lawsuits across 40 states against telehealth companies and compounding pharmacies.
entries.summary: Eli Lilly sues Empower Pharmacy and Strive over compounded tirzepatide

entries.content: GoodRx analysis highlights the stark pricing disparity that fueled the compounding boom: brand-name Ozempic lists at approximately $1,028/month and Wegovy at $1,349/month without insurance, while compounded semaglutide from telehealth providers cost $179-299/month, representing 70-80% savings. The FDA reported over 455 adverse events with compounded semaglutide and 320 with compounded tirzepatide by February 2025, raising safety questions about non-FDA-approved formulations. Post-shortage, some patients face difficult transitions as brand-name costs remain prohibitive without insurance, and the FDA acknowledged that treatment gaps and local shortages could persist even after the official shortage resolution.
entries.summary: Price gap: compounded semaglutide at $179-299/month vs brand-name at $998-1,349/month

entries.content: Despite the FDA's enforcement actions, Advisory Board reports that several companies found workarounds to continue offering compounded GLP-1 medications. Noom, Hims & Hers, and Mochi Health continued offering personalized doses, oral pills, gels, drops, and even gummy versions of GLP-1 drugs, arguing these modifications meet patient-specific needs under FDA regulations. Some companies add vitamin B12 or niacinamide, claiming reduced side effects and a clinically different product. The FDA escalated enforcement in February 2026 by announcing intent to restrict access to GLP-1 active pharmaceutical ingredients used in non-FDA-approved compounded products, and specifically warned it would use seizures and injunctions against non-compliant companies.
entries.summary: Compounders find workarounds despite FDA enforcement: modified doses, oral forms, and added ingredients

entries.content: On February 6, 2026, the FDA announced it would restrict access to semaglutide and tirzepatide APIs used in non-FDA-approved compounded drugs, specifically naming Hims & Hers in its enforcement announcement. The move came one day after Hims launched a $49/month compounded oral semaglutide product, and the FDA stated it would refer the company to the Department of Justice for potential violations of federal law. Hims shares fell over 14% in after-hours trading. The crackdown represented an unprecedented escalation, with FDA Commissioner Marty Makary highlighting Hims' Super Bowl ad for compounded GLP-1s that lacked any mention of side effects. By March 2026, Hims resolved the dispute by partnering with Novo Nordisk to offer branded semaglutide products instead.
entries.summary: FDA signals major crackdown: restricting GLP-1 ingredients for compounders, Hims shares tumble

entries.content: Unlike the US where compounding pharmacies filled the affordability gap, India is addressing GLP-1 access through generic manufacturing following semaglutide patent expiry on March 20, 2026. Over 40 Indian manufacturers are preparing launches, with Natco Pharma pricing its vial at Rs 1,290/month (nearly 90% below branded pricing) and Eris Lifesciences at Rs 220 per shot. India does not have a comparable 503A/503B compounding framework, so the generic pathway provides a regulated, scalable alternative. CareEdge Ratings projects the Indian GLP-1 market will grow from Rs 1,000-1,200 crore to Rs 4,500-5,000 crore by 2030, with Novo Nordisk preemptively cutting its India semaglutide price by 37% ahead of generic competition.
entries.summary: India takes a different path: generic manufacturing replaces compounding for affordable GLP-1 access
